y1: Seeing the crowds, Jesus went up on a mountain and sat down. In those days, teachers sat to teach. This showed that an authoritative teaching was beginning.
y2: Matthew's readers would remember Moses on Mount Sinai in this scene. Just as Moses received the Law on the mountain, Jesus teaches the life of the kingdom of heaven on the mountain.
y3: There are five great sermons in the Gospel of Matthew (chapters 5–7, 10, 13, 18, 24–25). This structure brings to mind the five books of the Torah. The Sermon on the Mount is the first and most famous of them.
y5: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Jesus declares “blessed” eight times.
y6: This is not a list of conditions saying, “if you do this, you will be blessed.” It is a declaration of blessedness stating that the kingdom of heaven is already open to such people.
y7: The first (5:3) and eighth (5:10) beatitudes end with the same words: “the kingdom of heaven is theirs.” All the blessings within this frame are about the kingdom of heaven. The first four are about poverty before God, and the last four are about a life directed toward one's neighbor.
y8: Salt that has lost its flavor
y9: “You are the salt of the world.” Salt was a valuable thing that gave flavor and protected meat from spoiling.
y10: The salt from near the Dead Sea contained impurities, and when its saltiness was gone, it became useless. When a disciple of Jesus becomes exactly like the world, they turn into salt that has lost its flavor.
y11: Jesus does not say “become salt,” He says “you are salt.” This is an identity already given. The issue is not whether to be salt or not, but not to lose the flavor.
y12: A light that cannot be hidden
y13: “You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden.” The villages on the Galilean hills could be seen from far away even at night.
y14: A small clay lamp would light up an entire one-room house. People who see our good deeds glorify the Father in heaven. This is not a light that boasts of itself, but a light that points to God.
y15: 5:16 says “let them see,” while 6:1 says “do not do them to be seen.” This is not a contradiction. The difference is in the purpose. If God is glorified, it is light; if I want to receive praise, it is a show.
verse: “Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”
prayer: Jesus, thank You for teaching a happiness different from the world's. Accept me, who is empty-handed before You. Help me to be salt that does not lose its flavor and a light that is not hidden, so that people may see the Father in heaven. I pray in the name of Jesus Christ. Amen.
d0: mountain. In the Bible, a mountain is a place where God speaks. It reminds us of Moses on Mount Sinai and Elijah on Mount Carmel. Traditionally, the hill near Capernaum is called the Mount of Beatitudes.
d1: poor in spirit. “Ptochos” means a poverty where one lives by begging. It is a person who knows they are empty-handed before God. A person who boasts in their own strength has no empty hands to receive the kingdom of heaven.
d2: blessed. It is not a good mood, but a state that God declares as “good.” In the Azerbaijani Bible, it is translated as “Nə bəxtiyardır …!” (How blessed is...!).
d3: salt. In an era without refrigerators, it was a valuable thing that protected meat and fish from spoiling. It was also a symbol of the covenant (Lev. 2:13). The village of Magdala in Galilee was famous for salting fish.
d4: light. Isaiah said that Israel would be a “light to the nations” (Isa. 49:6). Jesus gives this mission to His disciples. The “great light” in 4:16 now shines through the disciples.
d5: glorify. The Hebrew word “kavod” also means “weight.” It is the showing of how great God is. Our good deeds bring glory to God.
